8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":2,"verseId":2,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Motion","totalVerses":25,"verseData":{"id":"v2_2","number":2,"title":"The Opponent's Reply: Motion in the Moving","sanskrit":{"text":"ceṣṭā yatra gamanam tatraiva | gamyamāne ca ceṣṭā na gate nāgate ||","transliteration":"ceṣṭā yatra gamanam tatraiva | gamyamāne ca ceṣṭā na gate nāgate","translation":"Where there is change, there is motion. Since there is change in the moving, And not in the moved or not-moved, Motion is in that which is moving."},"philosophy":{"insight":"The opponent counters v.1 by placing motion in the present act of moving — the dynamic process itself, not in static past/future states. Nāgārjuna will dismantle this in v.3-11.","madhyamaka":"Garfield identifies this as the opponent's response to the trilemma: \"Obviously motion is in the presently moving!\" Kalupahana notes this reflects the common-sense Abhidharma view that the present dharma is the \"active\" one. But Nāgārjuna presents this view only to deconstruct it — the \"currently moving\" turns out to be just as problematic as past and future states.","quantum":"Schrödinger Equation (Unitary Evolution): The wave function |ψ(t)⟩ evolves continuously via iħ∂|ψ⟩/∂t = H|ψ⟩. Change is not in any single snapshot but in the continuous evolution itself — the process, not the state.","bridge":"The opponent's intuition maps to the Schrödinger picture: change is real and located in continuous evolution. But just as the wave function's evolution is not a \"thing\" that can be isolated from the system (it IS the system's description), motion cannot be isolated as a property separate from the mover.","accessible":"The opponent says: \"Motion is happening right NOW, in the thing that's currently moving!\" This seems obvious. A spinning top is spinning NOW. But Nāgārjuna will ask: what makes it a \"mover\" before the motion? This common-sense view will unravel.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, \"currently moving\" is perfectly meaningful. Ultimately, no inherent process of \"going\" can be located in the present moment apart from past and future states.","commonMisconception":"The opponent's view seems like common sense. Nāgārjuna doesn't deny present-moment experience — he shows it can't be established as INHERENTLY real."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Schrödinger Equation / Unitary Evolution","score":86,"strength":"High","explanation":"Continuous quantum evolution parallels the idea that change is in the process, but the evolution cannot be separated from the system itself.","caveat":"Structural parallel between process-disruption-by-analysis in both frameworks. Not a claim of physical identity."},"animation":{"geometry":"Evolving Wave Function","anchor":"A sinusoidal wave evolving in real-time along a horizontal axis. Clicking to freeze it shows this view collapses under scrutiny.","educationalGoal":"User sees that the 'present moment' of motion is unfindable — it's a conceptual knife-edge that dissolves under analysis."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Is Nāgārjuna agreeing here that motion is in \"that which is moving\"?","a":"No — he is presenting the opponent's counter-argument to v.1. It's the common-sense view: \"Obviously motion is happening NOW in the thing that's moving.\" But he sets this up precisely to demolish it in v.3-11.","realLifeExample":"In a debate, a lawyer might restate the opponent's strongest argument before showing why it fails. Nāgārjuna is doing exactly this — giving the opposing view its best expression before dismantling it."},{"q":"What is the significance of linking motion and change?","a":"It shifts the search from static endpoints (past/future) to the dynamic process itself. But this move creates a new problem: if \"the moving\" is what has change, this presupposes something already identified as \"moving\" — which requires motion. Circularity emerges.","realLifeExample":"Saying \"the runner runs\" seems informative. But \"runner\" already means \"one who runs.\" The statement is secretly circular — it presupposes what it claims to explain."},{"q":"How does the Schrödinger equation model this \"change in the moving\"?","a":"The Schrödinger equation iħ∂|ψ⟩/∂t = H|ψ⟩ describes how a quantum state evolves continuously over time. The evolution IS the change — it's not a property added to a static state. Similarly, the opponent says motion IS the change happening in the presently moving thing. But in quantum mechanics, the wave function's evolution cannot be separated from the system — there's no \"thing\" plus \"its evolution.\"","realLifeExample":"A river's flow isn't separate from the river. The flowing IS what makes it a river. But you can't point to \"the flowing\" as a separate thing you could remove. The flow and the river are inseparable."},{"q":"Why will this view fail in the next verses?","a":"Because calling something \"the moving\" already presupposes motion (v.3). If you need motion to identify \"the mover,\" but motion is supposed to be IN the mover, you have a vicious circle. Neither motion nor mover can be established first — they're mutually dependent, hence empty of independent existence.","realLifeExample":"What makes an employee an \"employee\"? The job. What makes a job a \"job\"? That someone (an employee) does it. Neither concept exists independently — each requires the other."},{"q":"Does quantum mechanics have the same circularity problem?","a":"Yes, in the measurement problem. The wave function describes a system's evolution, but to confirm the evolution, you need to measure — which collapses the wave function. The act of checking the evolution changes it. You can't isolate \"the evolving\" from the observation context.","realLifeExample":"Asking \"Are you asleep?\" wakes someone up. The question (observation) destroys the state (sleep) it's trying to verify. You can't confirm sleep while checking for it."},{"q":"How does this verse connect the Abhidharma context?","a":"The Sarvāstivādins held that dharmas in all three times are real, but only present dharmas have \"activity\" (kāritra). The opponent here appeals to this — motion is the activity of the present dharma. Nāgārjuna will show that even this \"present activity\" cannot be established inherently, undermining the Sarvāstivādin framework.","deeper":"Kalupahana notes this verse bridges Abhidharma realism and Nāgārjuna's anti-realism. The opponent's best move (locating motion in present activity) becomes the very thing that collapses."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"Whose view is presented in verse 2?","options":["A) Nāgārjuna's final conclusion","B) The opponent's counter-argument that motion is in the currently moving thing","C) The Buddha's teaching on impermanence","D) A Western philosopher's view"],"correct":"B","explanation":"Verse 2 presents the opponent's response to the trilemma: motion is not in the past or future states, but in the presently moving thing. Nāgārjuna will challenge this in subsequent verses."},"intermediate":{"question":"What does the Schrödinger equation describe?","options":["A) How particles collide","B) How quantum states evolve continuously over time","C) How to build a quantum computer","D) How to measure spin"],"correct":"B","explanation":"The Schrödinger equation describes the continuous evolution of a quantum state over time — the change IS the process, not a property added to a static thing."},"advanced":{"question":"Why does locating motion in \"the moving\" create a circularity problem?","options":["A) Because \"the moving\" is undefined","B) Because identifying something as \"the moving\" already presupposes motion, so motion cannot then be explained by reference to \"the moving\"","C) Because nothing moves","D) Because time doesn't exist"],"correct":"B","explanation":"To call something \"the moving\" requires already identifying motion in it. But if motion is supposed to be explained by being IN \"the moving,\" the explanation is circular — each concept presupposes the other."}},"verseText":"Where there is change, there is motion.
